title: HCLTech Java Developer — core Java, then architecture, then the manager
excerpt: Four stages from a recruiter screen through Core Java, a systems-and-architecture round, and a techno-managerial close. Package above 17 LPA.
body:
## Background
Four distinct stages, moving along steadily from the initial screening through to the final managerial round. I had 3+ years of experience at the time.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Screening call
A short initial check — the recruiter went over my profile at a high level, asked about my **notice period**, and threw in a few basic technical questions to confirm I was a reasonable fit before moving forward.

### 2. Technical round 1 — Core Java
**HashMaps**, the distinction between **interfaces and abstract classes**, and **Java 8 Streams**. There was also a coding challenge worked into this round, to see how I applied these concepts in practice rather than just how well I could explain them.

### 3. Technical round 2 — Architecture & systems
A step up in scope: **system architecture**, **Spring Security**, **microservices**, database management, and a discussion around troubleshooting issues in a **production environment** — the kind of practical "what would you actually do" scenarios rather than textbook questions.

### 4. Techno-managerial round
Team dynamics, how I approach problem-solving in a team setting, a few behavioural situations, and how I'd handle managing project requirements day to day.

## Verdict
**Selected** — Java Developer, package exceeding **17 LPA**.

title: EY Tech Consultant — where the HR round is the real eliminator
excerpt: An OA, a verbal communication round, a practical technical interview, and an HR round that turned out to be an eliminator rather than a formality.
body:
## Round-by-round

### 1. Online assessment
Numerical and logical reasoning, plus a coding question in the easy-to-medium range.

### 2. Verbal communication round
More of a language assessment — a mix of listening-based tasks and a speaking component.

### 3. Technical interview
Heavily focused on **real-world application** rather than definitions:
- **OOP** principles in practical terms
- **DSA** — specifically **HashMaps**
- **DBMS** — normalisation and SQL
- A detailed discussion of a **Java** project I'd built, where I had to justify my design choices in depth

### 4. HR round
This turned out to be an **eliminator round**, not a formality. It covered how genuine my interest in the technical side of the role was, the difference between a **developer and a consultant**, and a puzzle-based question meant to test problem-solving under pressure.

## Verdict
**Selected** — Tech Consultant.

title: Expedia SDE-2 — quiet job hunt, then back-to-back CodePair rounds
excerpt: Structured prep on DSA and design, a slow start to the job search, then a three-question OA and two back-to-back live coding rounds on Zoom.
body:
## Background
My preparation was fairly structured — **DSA**, **Low-Level Design** and basic **High-Level Design**, while staying grounded in my primary stack, **Java Spring Boot**.

The job search itself was tougher than I expected. Despite sending out a good number of applications, the calls just weren't coming. Around the time this process picked up I was also juggling a separate offer I'd already received from another company, so I had to balance that alongside actively interviewing here.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Online assessment
Three **DSA** questions, all at medium difficulty — a mix of **graph** and **DP** problems.

### 2. Technical round 1
Over **Zoom** using **CodePair**, focused on live coding and DSA problem-solving.

### 3. Technical round 2
Followed immediately after in the same back-to-back format, again centred on coding and DSA.

## Verdict
**Selected** — SDE-2.

title: Google L4 — strong start, fell short on the DP round
excerpt: Recruiter outreach in December, phone screen, three virtual onsites and Googliness. Two rounds went well, a hard DP round did not.
body:
## How I applied
A recruiter reached out on **LinkedIn** in December — a 15–16 minute call covering open roles, my background, a self-rating on DSA (I said ~8/10) and availability. Prep resources, a rough schedule and a mock-interview group followed.

## Timeline
1. Recruiter screening call
2. Technical phone screen
3. 3 onsite technical rounds (virtual)
4. Googliness round

## Round-by-round

### 1. Phone screen
Given a grid-like matrix plus a list of items and quantities, arrange items so similar ones end up adjacent row-wise or column-wise. It looked like a graph problem but was really about spotting the right pattern. Talked through the approach, coded it, discussed complexity — finished on schedule.

### 2. Onsite 1 — Dependency graph
Framed as managing storage disks and snapshots: a snapshot can only be removed once all disks (and disks derived from them) are deleted. Output a valid deletion order. Took some back-and-forth to understand, then solved it cleanly.

### 3. Onsite 2 — Dynamic programming
2D boxes of varying dimensions; find the maximum number that can be nested. A genuinely tough DP problem. I only reached brute force in the time available, and I knew while explaining it that it wasn't what they wanted.

### 4. Onsite 3 — Sorting / binary search
A neighbourhood of blocks with houses of different colours; rearrange so each block has uniquely coloured houses in sorted order. I got to something workable but not optimal. With a couple of minutes left it clicked that **binary search** was the key — too late.

### 5. Googliness
Relaxed conversation about background, projects and behavioural questions. A nice change of pace, and it went well.

## Verdict
**Not selected.**

title: Amazon SDE-1 — second attempt, with a referral
excerpt: A previous rejection, then a referral and ~6 months of experience. OA on HackerRank plus a workplace simulation, then three rounds.
body:
## Background
Not my first attempt at Amazon — I'd tried before without success. I applied again in January with a referral from a friend, with about six months of professional experience.

## Online assessment
The invite came in March: two DSA questions on HackerRank, a one-hour workplace simulation (a distinctive part of Amazon's process), and behavioural questions.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1
Two DSA problems plus discussion tied to the **Leadership Principles**.

### Round 2
Purely technical, with DSA a step up in difficulty from Round 1.

### Round 3 — Managerial
A blend of everything: a DSA component, more Leadership Principles discussion, and a deeper conversation about my resume and background.

## Verdict
An official offer came about a week after the final round. **Selected.**

title: Zomato SDE-1 on-campus — an Air Force internship that stood out
excerpt: A hard 90-minute OA, then HLD around my own projects, core CS fundamentals, and an HR round.
body:
## Background
An on-campus hiring drive. Eligibility required a CGPA of 7+ and was open to all branches.

## Round-by-round

### Online assessment
90 minutes, three problems, all at hard/competitive-programming level — two **dynamic programming** based, and a third combining **binary search** with **DFS**.

### Technical round 1
Centred on high-level design around the projects I'd built. I'd also done an internship with the **Indian Air Force**, which turned out to be a genuine conversation-starter and stood out as something different from the usual resume. There was also a DSA problem — a variation on the classic coin-change type.

### Technical round 2
Core CS fundamentals — Operating Systems, DBMS and SQL.

### HR round
Cultural fit and communication skills in a more conversational format.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Amazon SDE-1 off-campus — a loop that ran February to July
excerpt: Applied in November, loop started in February and stretched to July. OA plus three rounds. Joined the Amazon Music team.
body:
## Background
I applied off-campus in November, but the loop didn't start until February and ran to July. Amazon seems to hold on to promising profiles and revisit them when an opening appears rather than closing them out.

## Online assessment
Two DSA problems plus a separate work-style/behavioural assessment. For the work-style section I kept answers aligned with Amazon's **Leadership Principles**.

## Round format
Roughly 45 minutes of coding (usually two problems, medium to medium-hard) followed by 10–15 minutes of Leadership Principles questions.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1
A 2D matrix/graph problem, plus a second question needing a **line sweep** approach.

### Round 2 — first attempt
A string problem alongside one requiring a **monotonic stack**.

### Round 2 — repeated
Rescheduling on their end meant this round was redone from scratch, and it was noticeably tougher: a **priority queue** problem plus a design question in the spirit of a bill-splitting app.

### Round 3 — final
Conducted by a principal engineer, with no coding at all. Entirely focused on past experience, internship projects and the reasoning behind specific design choices.

## Verdict
**Selected** — joined the Amazon Music team.

title: Zomato SDE-1 — an internal opening found through a referral
excerpt: A whiteboard DSA and DBMS round, a system design round that became a database deep dive, HR, and a final CTO conversation.
body:
## Background
I got in through an internal opening thanks to a referral from a friend. The role wasn't listed on any public job portal — it only came my way through that connection, which made me realise how much networking with seniors and peers matters for off-campus hiring.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA & DBMS
Conducted on a whiteboard and fairly open-ended rather than standard, repetitive problems. Core topics were **topological sorting** and **dynamic programming**. Partway through I proactively mentioned that I intended to keep running my startup and YouTube channel alongside the role, just to be transparent up front.

### Round 2 — System design
Not a typical system design format. It pivoted into a deep discussion of my previous internship experience, digging into database concepts — **SQL vs NoSQL**, indexing and sharding.

### Round 3 — HR
More conversational, centred on my future goals and what specifically drew me to Zomato.

### Final round — CTO discussion
A candid one-on-one with the CTO focused on my broader achievements.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: PhonePe SDE-1 — machine coding, code review, DSA and hiring manager
excerpt: Reached out to a recruiter on LinkedIn. A full working Java application in the machine coding round, then a review of that same code.
body:
## Background
I reached out to a recruiter on **LinkedIn** and got the opportunity from there.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Machine coding
Submitting a fully functional **Java application** rather than solving an isolated problem.

### Round 2 — Explanation / code review
Walking the interviewer through the code I'd submitted in the machine coding round, and being ready to modify or extend it on the spot based on their questions.

### Round 3 — DSA
Two to three algorithmic problems covering linked lists, binary search and graphs.

### Round 4 — Hiring manager
A blend of past projects, deeper technical questions and behavioural questions.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: HCLTech on-campus — 90 MCQs, a GD that wasn't a GD, and two resume-driven tech rounds
excerpt: A campus drive with a 60%+ eligibility bar: aptitude MCQs with fill-in-the-logic coding, an online group discussion, two technical interviews, and HR.
body:
## Background
This came through a **campus drive** at my college. The application itself required filling in personal details and uploading documents carefully, and the general eligibility bar was **60%+ in both 10th and 12th**.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Online assessment
**90 MCQs** covering aptitude — logical, arithmetic and verbal reasoning — along with two coding snippets where I had to fill in missing logic rather than write something from scratch (reversing a number, counting characters in a string).

### 2. Group discussion
Conducted online, and despite the name it didn't feel like a debate-style GD — it was much more about gauging **communication and confidence**. The interviewer asked fairly personal questions: a self-introduction, questions about hobbies. I answered honestly here, since follow-ups tend to expose anything exaggerated pretty quickly.

### 3–4. Technical interviews
Two separate one-on-one rounds. Both stayed close to my resume — my **projects**, along with **Java**, **C**, **SQL**, **DBMS** and **Operating Systems** concepts. I made sure I could speak to every detail of my projects in depth, since that's where most of the questioning concentrated.

### 5. HR interview
Document verification, plus a conversation about my flexibility with **shift timings** and **work location**, and a few basic questions about the company. I stayed flexible and positive throughout.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Google L3 Software Engineer — referral to offer
excerpt: Referral via LinkedIn, then a recruiter call, phone screen, three DSA onsites and a Googliness round. Selected for L3.
body:
## How I applied
I was referred after reaching out on **LinkedIn** and sharing my resume.

## Timeline
1. Recruiter call — role, background, logistics
2. Technical phone screen (DSA)
3. Onsite loop — 3 DSA rounds
4. Googliness (behavioural / culture fit)

## Round-by-round

### 1. Recruiter call
Unexpectedly technical for an intro call — complexity of Bubble Sort and how heap operations work at a high level. Don't treat this as a pure logistics call; keep fundamentals warm from day one.

### 2. Technical phone screen
A **graph** problem. Not the hardest of the loop, but clearly designed to filter anyone without solid traversal basics.

### 3. Onsite 1 — Strings
String manipulation. The interviewer mostly watched how cleanly I handled edge cases while parsing/transforming.

### 4. Onsite 2 — Optimisation (Bucket Sort)
The toughest round for me. I first solved it with **heaps** at O(n log n); the interviewer kept pushing for better. Thinking out loud, I reached a **bucket sort** solution — constant time for this specific problem. Really a test of how far you can optimise a working solution under pressure.

### 5. Onsite 3 — Range queries
Hardest round of the loop: range queries on an array, with a follow-up that needed **binary search** to make querying efficient.

### 6. Googliness
A conversation rather than an interrogation — background, deep dive into projects and my exact contribution, and why Google specifically.

## Verdict
**Selected for L3.**

title: Microsoft SDE-2 — rounds anchored to my own past projects
excerpt: Referral-driven application. LLD and scaling rounds both built on my own project work rather than generic prompts.
body:
## Background
Rather than applying through the standard portal, I reached out directly to recruiters and leaned on referrals — that route worked better for getting noticed.

## Online coding round
On HackerRank, two problems in 90 minutes. Clearing it came down to passing as many test cases as possible to hit the internal cutoff score.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1
Medium-level problems. The interviewer expected a fully optimised solution rather than brute force; once I had it, the conversation moved to space complexity and then my past projects.

### Round 2 — Low-level design
Instead of a standalone design prompt, the interviewer asked me to walk through class diagrams and relationships based directly on one of my own past projects.

### Round 3 — System design / scaling
Also anchored to my own project work, but focused on scalability concepts and the **CAP theorem**, and how those applied to what I'd built.

### Round 4 — Behavioural
Workplace scenarios — navigating conflicts with a manager or colleague. One question: looking back, what could you have done differently to convince your manager? I made sure to have real, specific stories ready rather than answering in the abstract.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: EY — AMCAT cutoff, two scenario-driven tech rounds, then the client
excerpt: An AMCAT assessment with a 65% cutoff, two technical rounds on Java/Spring Boot/microservices and SQL/AWS, and a client round on past project work.
body:
## Background
Three years of experience, interviewing for a Java-based engineering role.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Online assessment
Conducted on the **AMCAT** platform. Clearing it required scoring at least **65%**.

### 2. Technical round 1
**Java**, **Spring Boot** and **microservices**, with a mix of coding tasks and scenario-based questions rather than pure theory.

### 3. Technical round 2
Same vein, going deeper into **SQL** and **AWS** — again combining hands-on coding with practical, scenario-driven questions.

### 4. Client round
Shifted focus entirely to my previous project experience, with the client wanting a detailed understanding of the work I'd actually done.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: PhonePe SDE Intern + FTE — 800 applicants, 29 shortlisted
excerpt: A 90-minute OA of four LeetCode-hard problems. Interviewers cared more about communication than immediate optimality.
body:
## Eligibility & online assessment
Open to CS/IT branches with a CGPA cutoff of 9.35+.

The OA saw about 800 applicants, of which 29 were shortlisted. It ran 90 minutes with four **LeetCode Hard**-level problems. The bar was roughly 16 of 40 total test cases across the set — full solutions on every problem weren't necessary to make the cut.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA
Two problems: one graph-based, another a tree scenario needing a **binary lifting** approach. The interviewer wanted me to start with brute force before working toward something optimised, rather than jumping straight to the best approach.

### Round 2 — Technical deep dive
Difficulty stepped up with two harder problems touching **binary search** and graph patterns. As in Round 1, the interviewer cared more about how clearly I communicated my problem-solving process than about arriving at the optimal solution immediately.

### Round 3 — HR & behavioural
A detailed discussion of my main personal project (an AI-based learning platform), past internship experience, and a basic database schema design exercise around a social-media-style scenario.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Capgemini Analyst (fresher) — 30 minutes on Superset, and a GenAI project that carried it
excerpt: A single 25–30 minute round on Superset mixing HR and technical questions, where a personal Generative AI project added the depth that rehearsed answers couldn't.
body:
## Background
The whole thing happened on the **Superset** platform and wrapped up in about 25–30 minutes — quick as these things go, but it still covered a good amount of ground.

## Round-by-round

### Introduction
I kept it tight, 50–60 seconds: academics plus a couple of things I was proud of outside coursework.

### HR territory
Strengths and weaknesses — I backed both with actual examples instead of listing traits. A self-rating on **teamwork**, and a **decision-making** question that asked me to walk through a real situation rather than theorise about one.

### Technical
**Java** first, then core OOP — **Inheritance** and **Polymorphism** specifically.

### Project discussion
The most interesting part. The conversation turned to a personal project I'd built involving **Generative AI**, and I could tell it genuinely worked in my favour — it gave the interview more depth than rehearsed answers, and I think it's part of why things went the way they did.

## Verdict
**Selected** — Analyst role, 4.25 LPA (4 LPA base + 25K bonus).

title: Microsoft SDE-3 Friday Drive — positive feedback, no further rounds
excerpt: Applied via the careers portal. Cleared coding and LLD with positive feedback, but the process didn't continue past interview day.
body:
## Background
I applied directly through Microsoft's careers portal for a Senior Software Engineer (SDE-3) opening.

## Online assessment
A coding assessment leaning heavily on **monotonic stack** and **sliding window** techniques.

## Interview format
Scheduled as part of what Microsoft calls a **"Friday Drive"** — back-to-back slots packed into a single day rather than spread over weeks.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Coding & problem solving (9:00–10:00)
Core DSA. The main problem was a variant of "Longest Substring with At Least K Repeating Characters" (LeetCode 395). Midway through, a situational design question: model an organisational hierarchy (a CEO with multiple layers of reports) using the most suitable data structure.

### Round 2 — Low-level design (10:30–11:30)
Object-oriented design of a system similar to Zomato — core entities, relationships between classes, functional requirements and edge cases. I stayed in the driver's seat, walking the happy path first before exceptions rather than waiting to be prompted.

### Round 3 — High-level design (scheduled)
Planned to cover load balancers and caching strategies. I didn't reach this stage.

### Round 4 — Behavioural / managerial (scheduled)
Expected to cover past challenges and conflicts in **STAR** format. Also not reached.

## Outcome
Positive feedback after both Round 1 and Round 2, but the process didn't move beyond the initial interview day.

**Not selected (post Round 2).**

title: Amazon India SDE-1 — OA to offer in a few weeks
excerpt: A fast loop: resume + DSA, a low-level design round, and a Bar Raiser centred on Leadership Principles.
body:
## Background
This moved quickly — from OA to final result in a few weeks.

## Online assessment
DSA-heavy with a behavioural component. I kept my responses honest and straightforward rather than trying to game it.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Resume & DSA
A resume walkthrough plus a coding problem. The problem was math-heavy; solving it efficiently needed **binary search** with the **Sieve of Eratosthenes**, plus further optimisation.

### Round 2 — Low-level design
Design the architecture for a streaming service. Getting to an efficient design came down to using **HashMaps** and **HashSets** in the right places.

### Round 3 — Bar Raiser
The toughest round — managerial, entirely around Amazon's **Leadership Principles**. It works as a checkpoint on whether you'd genuinely raise the bar versus the existing team, not just be an acceptable hire.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Microsoft SDE-1 off-campus — Tic-Tac-Toe LLD and a URL shortener
excerpt: Three same-day rounds of about 45 minutes each: LLD with a game-tree follow-up, a URL-shortening system design, and a managerial round on networking fundamentals.
body:
## Background
I applied directly through the Microsoft careers portal using a referral from a senior contact.

## Resume shortlisting
My internship experience at a couple of well-known tech companies seemed to carry real weight at this stage.

## Online assessment
Coding problems around two medium and one hard. To clear it I needed to solve them completely rather than partially.

## Round-by-round
*(All three rounds on the same day, roughly 45 minutes each.)*

### Technical round 1 — Low-level design
Design a simple two-player grid-based game (think Tic-Tac-Toe): class structure, relationships, and how game state would be managed. The follow-up was to extend it with logic for the optimal move at any state, which meant a game-tree-based decision algorithm.

There was also a coding question on rotating a 2D matrix — **in place**, modifying the original rather than creating a new one.

### Technical round 2 — System design
Designing a large-scale **URL-shortening service**: how the mapping between short and long URLs works, handling billions of unique addresses, what hashing strategy makes sense, and edge cases at that scale.

### Managerial round
Technical and behavioural. On the technical side, networking fundamentals — DNS, HTTP, the three-way handshake, TLS/SSL. On the behavioural side, academic background and internships in more depth.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Accenture Java Developer — one long technical round built around microservices
excerpt: A single deep technical round covering microservices communication, REST design and live Stream API coding, then a short HR conversation.
body:
## Background
Two rounds — a technical interview followed by HR. The technical round ran fairly long and covered a lot of ground, so I'll break it down by topic, which is roughly how the conversation flowed.

## Technical round

### Microservices
The interviewer's main focus for a good chunk of the round. How microservices actually **communicate** with each other, **asynchronous messaging**, and a step-by-step walkthrough of how I'd build a microservices-based application starting from nothing.

### REST APIs
Flowed naturally from the microservices discussion — different ways of sending data to a server, **`@PathVariable` vs `@RequestParam`**, and how I'd implement **GET, POST and PUT** in a real service.

### Core Java — Stream API
The most hands-on part. I was asked to write code in my IDE to retrieve employee phone number details using **Java Streams**, then explain why **`.collect()`** matters there — not just what it does syntactically, but why it's the right tool for pulling the final result together.

### Functional concepts
**Functional interfaces** and **lambda expressions**, with quick code examples for both written on the spot.

### Project experience
Some time on my actual project work — specifically the architectural challenges I'd run into and how I worked through them.

## HR round
Much shorter and general: why I was leaving my current company, what drew me to Accenture, compensation expectations, and whether I was open to relocating.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Microsoft SDE with 2.5 years experience — five rounds from a LinkedIn message
excerpt: Reverse a linked list in groups of K, a logging framework LLD, an arcade-game HLD, and a word-chaining problem in the hiring manager round.
body:
## Background
It started with a **LinkedIn** message — a Microsoft recruiter asking if I'd be open to interviewing. I was serving my notice period, so it felt worth exploring.

I finished my B.Tech in Computer Science in 2021, then joined a networking/telecom company as a Software Engineer working mostly in C/C++, with some Python, Bash and YANG. After about two and a half years I was ready for a change.

## Round-by-round
*(Five rounds in total.)*

### Round 1 — Online coding
A test link from the recruiter. The problems sat in the easy-to-medium range. Clearing it led to a call to move forward.

### Round 2 — Technical (1 hour)
After introductions, straight into problem solving:
- Reverse a **linked list in groups of size K**, each set reversed in place.
- Find the element in an array appearing more than n/2 times.

### Round 3 — Low-level design (1 hour)
Design a **logging framework** from scratch: multiple log levels (debug, info, error), different appenders attachable per level, and support for changing the log level or adding appenders dynamically at runtime.

### Round 4 — High-level design (1 hour)
Designing a well-known arcade-style game from a system/architecture standpoint, plus a transaction design for an e-commerce scenario.

### Round 5 — Hiring manager (1 hour)
Technical and non-technical:
- A **word chaining** problem — whether a set of words can be linked in sequence, where a word chains to the next only if its last three characters exactly match the first three of the following word.
- The rest went in depth on specific projects from my previous role.

## Verdict
HR called four days after the final round. **Selected.**

title: Amazon SDE-2 with 3 years experience — DSA, LLD, HLD, Bar Raiser
excerpt: Four loop rounds mixing in-person and virtual. Leadership Principles came up in every single round.
body:
## Background
The process opened with an OA covering DSA, behavioural questions and a system design component. After clearing it I moved into four loop rounds, a mix of in-person and virtual.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Coding / DSA
Fairly standard territory — graphs, DP, arrays and strings. The interviewer wanted more than a working solution: it had to be syntactically clean, and I had to handle follow-up constraints added as the conversation went on.

### Round 2 — Low-level design
Requirement gathering, then API design and schema design. Doing well came down to solid OOP fundamentals and the right design patterns, backed by class and UML diagrams.

### Round 3 — High-level design & hiring manager
Define requirements up front, then estimate scale — expected users, queries per second, database size — and justify every design decision, including caching strategy and the overall logical flow.

### Round 4 — Bar Raiser
Conducted by someone from a completely different team, evaluating performance holistically. A mix of HLD, LLD and DSA, and I was expected to produce fully functional, tested code rather than pseudocode.

## A note on Leadership Principles
These weren't confined to one round — one or two came up in every session, always tied back to real experiences from my background.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Zomato SDE off-campus — competitive-programming style rounds and a VP chat
excerpt: Two technical interviews followed by an in-person round at the Gurugram office.
body:
## Background
Three main rounds — two technical interviews followed by an in-person round at Zomato's Gurugram office.

## Round-by-round

### Technical round 1
Four coding questions in total, mostly leaning toward competitive-programming-style problems rather than typical interview questions.

### Technical round 2
A DSA coding question combined with a low-level design problem — designing a **library management system** — along with a set of CS fundamentals questions.

### Final round — VP discussion
With Zomato's VP, noticeably more relaxed and conversational than the earlier technical rounds.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Amazon SDE-2 — an offer after years of trying
excerpt: Roughly three rejections and several cooling-off periods before this one. DSA, LLD, HLD and a Bar Raiser round.
body:
## Background
This offer didn't come easily — years of trying and more than three rejections, each with its own cooling-off period before I felt ready to try again. Eventually a recruiter reached out on **LinkedIn** about an SDE-2 opening.

## Online assessment
Three parts: a DSA coding section, a system design case study, and a behavioural component.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA
Graph problems requiring both **BFS** and **Dijkstra's algorithm**.

### Round 2 — Low-level design
Class diagrams and applying the relevant design patterns.

### Round 3 — High-level design
Functional and non-functional requirements, choosing an appropriate database, and operational excellence considerations.

### Round 4 — Bar Raiser
The most demanding round: a deep dive into problem solving that tested fundamentals including **binary search** and **topological sort**.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: PhonePe SDE-2 (~54 LPA) — stopped at the DSA round
excerpt: A 90-minute e-commerce machine coding round went fine; a competitive-programming-level graph problem in the DSA round did not.
body:
## Background
An SDE-2 opening with a package of roughly 54 LPA, structured across four rounds. I applied via referral.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Machine coding
90 minutes centred on **low-level design**: design an e-commerce application similar in spirit to a large online shopping platform, writing actual executable code while applying relevant design patterns. Followed by a 30-minute evaluation and discussion of what I'd built.

### Round 2 — DSA
60 minutes, two problems. The first was a genuinely tough **graph** problem at competitive-programming difficulty, which I struggled with. The second was a **dynamic programming** problem.

### Round 3 — High-level design (not reached)
I'd prepared for it but didn't progress far enough.

### Round 4 — Managerial (not reached)
Part of the overall process, but I didn't reach this stage either.

## Verdict
**Not selected** — did not progress past the DSA round.

title: EY Python Developer — five rounds including a client-facing one
excerpt: HR screen, a deep Python fundamentals round, a managerial deep-dive on projects, a client round, and a final HR round for negotiation.
body:
## Background
A lateral move at 3–5 years of experience. The whole process took a few weeks from start to finish, moving through a fairly standard set of stages for this level.

## Round-by-round

### 1. HR screening
A short preliminary call — communication, salary expectations, and how well my resume lined up with the role.

### 2. Technical round 1
Heavily on **Python** fundamentals: **decorators**, **generators**, the **GIL**, **multithreading**, and **deep vs shallow copy**, along with core OOP concepts. Then basic **SQL** (joins, `GROUP BY`) and API concepts using **Flask/Django**, including **JWT**-based authentication.

### 3. Technical / managerial round 2
Deep into my actual project experience — the architecture decisions I'd made, how I approach problem-solving on the job, and how I'd handled technical challenges or tight deadlines in the past.

### 4. Client round
The role was tied to a specific client, so this round focused on client-facing experience — requirement gathering and navigating conflicts within a team.

### 5. Final HR round
Salary negotiation, the finer details of the offer, and onboarding next steps.

## Verdict
**Selected** — Python Developer.

title: Microsoft SDE-2 — one online round plus four rounds in a single day
excerpt: Sequential rounds with no second chances: DSA, LLD, an unusual trees-and-queues problem, and system design with a partner-level interviewer.
body:
## Process overview
Five rounds in total — one standalone online coding round, then four back-to-back rounds condensed into a single day.

## Online coding round
DSA-heavy, on a platform similar to HackerRank. Two problems between medium and hard. To clear it you need to **fully** solve at least one including all hidden test cases; partial credit across both isn't enough.

## The "big day"
The remaining four rounds all landed on one day (typically a Friday or Saturday slot). Each round is sequential — you must clear one before the next, with no skipping ahead and no second chance if you stumble early.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA
Pure DSA, leaning hard toward the difficult end: a mix of **dynamic programming and graphs**. No warm-up at all.

### Round 2 — LLD / DSA
This round can go either way depending on the interviewer. Mine was an **LLD** discussion: clarify requirements first, walk through the design, then handle cross-questioning — especially on why I'd chosen C++ and how language-specific decisions played into the design.

### Round 3 — DSA
A genuinely unusual problem built around **trees and queues**. Not something I recognised from practice platforms, so it was less about recalling a pattern and more about reasoning through something unfamiliar under time pressure.

### Round 4 — System design + resume deep dive
With a partner-level interviewer, combining a deep dive into my work experience with a **system design** problem. Less a puzzle, more a conversation about how I think and what I've built.

## Verdict
Cleared all five rounds. **Selected.**

title: PhonePe SDE-1 on-campus — the whole process in about six hours
excerpt: Four rounds in a single day, including pen-and-paper technical rounds and an hour-long HR round covering OS and DBMS.
body:
## Background
The entire process wrapped up in a single day — roughly six hours across four rounds.

## Round-by-round

### Online assessment
Four fairly challenging problems focused on **dynamic programming** and **graphs**. I fully solved one and passed partial test cases on a second.

### Technical round 1
A one-on-one, pen-and-paper style round with two problems in the medium to medium-hard range — one involving prefix/suffix logic, the other a graph problem solvable with **BFS**.

### Technical round 2
Similar format, but the difficulty stepped up again — **dynamic programming** plus another BFS-based problem.

### HR round
The longest round, over an hour, covering:
- A deep dive into a MERN-stack project including backend architecture and data flow
- Core CS subjects, particularly **Operating Systems** (deadlocks, synchronisation) and **DBMS**
- Behavioural questions on leadership experience, why PhonePe specifically, and how I'd approach my first two weeks

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Expedia SDE-1 — behavioural OA, DSA, and an ML-heavy second interview
excerpt: Final-year CS student at NIT Jaipur: a two-hour behavioural OA, a technical test, a thorough DSA interview, and a 1.5-hour round with an ML engineer.
body:
## Background
Final-year CS student at **NIT Jaipur**. The role was SDE-1 via a summer internship — ₹40,000/month stipend, converting to a full-time CTC of **40 LPA**.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Online assessment
Two hours, and mostly **behavioural and critical thinking** questions rather than pure technical content.

### Round 2 — Technical test
One hour covering **DSA**, aptitude and CS fundamentals together. On the DSA side I worked through problems involving **prefix sums** and **binary search**.

### Round 3 — First interview
The interviewer had close to **18 years** of experience, which made the round feel especially thorough. Two DSA problems — one built around the **sliding window / two-pointer** technique, and a variation of the classic **trapping rain water** problem — plus a set of behavioural questions.

### Round 4 — Second interview
A longer, 1.5-hour round with a **Machine Learning** engineer. My resume leaned heavily into ML, and the questions reflected that: **PCA** and **LDA** concepts, some **system design**, and DSA including a question involving **Kadane's algorithm**.

## Verdict
**Selected** — SDE-1 internship converting to 40 LPA.

title: Microsoft SDE-2 Frontend — DSA, JS fundamentals and a collaborative editor design
excerpt: A Saturday hiring drive with all four rounds in one day. Offer extended at the L62 level.
body:
## Background
A recruiter reached out on **LinkedIn** about a Frontend-focused SDE-2 opening. I have 4+ years of experience.

## Online assessment
A HackerRank assessment with two DSA problems, both medium-to-hard.

## Hiring drive
Shortlisted for a Saturday drive with all four rounds packed into a single day.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA & JavaScript
Two parts. The DSA portion was a medium **graph** problem. The JavaScript portion involved working with **Date** objects to build a calendar view.

### Round 2 — Frontend fundamentals
Fast-moving: rapid-fire conceptual questions, output-based questions (predicting what a snippet prints), and a debugging exercise finding the issue without a debugger. I was also asked to build a custom hook to handle a dynamic form.

### Round 3 — System design
A high-level design discussion on building a **collaborative editor** — a real-time, multi-user document tool. The focus was heavily on trade-offs between architectural approaches rather than one "correct" design.

### Round 4 — Behavioural & technical
With a Group Engineering Manager. Career aspirations on the behavioural side; on the technical side, the architecture of a file uploader.

## Verdict
**Selected** — offer extended at the **L62** level.

title: Capgemini 2024 on-campus — a conversation, not an interrogation
excerpt: One interview covering MERN projects, an internship, Java/OOP basics, and behavioural questions that needed real examples rather than definitions.
body:
## Background
On-campus, 2024. It started casually — instead of the usual "tell me about yourself", the interviewer just asked how I was doing. That small shift set the tone: it felt less like an interrogation and more like a chat from the first minute.

## Round-by-round

### Projects and internship
I walked through what I'd built on the **MERN** stack, focusing on the real-world side rather than listing technologies — what problems it solved, and the difficulties I ran into. We then spent time on my internship and what I actually did day to day.

### Technical
Rooted in **Java** and **OOP** — function **overloading vs overriding** came up, which I was expecting, so that part felt comfortable.

### Behavioural
This caught me a little off guard. The classic **hard work vs smart work** question, which I had to back with an actual example rather than a definition, plus a team-based scenario testing how I'd navigate a tricky situation with colleagues. Nothing outrageous, but it made me think on my feet more than the technical questions did. The standard **"why Capgemini"** was in there too, and I'd prepared for it.

## Takeaway
The moments where I didn't fully know an answer taught me the most — staying calm and simply admitting it landed a lot better than trying to bluff.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Accenture Java Developer — deep Core Java and Hibernate, still a no
excerpt: Two rounds going properly deep into Core Java internals, exception handling, Spring Boot and Hibernate. It didn't convert.
body:
## Background
3.3 years of experience, interviewing for a Java Developer role. Two rounds.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — Core Java
Fundamentals in good depth:
- Method **overloading vs overriding**
- How **private and static methods** behave with visibility and inheritance, and access modifiers
- How the **JVM** works, Java's **platform independence**, and the **String Pool** mechanism
- **Exception handling** — checked vs unchecked, writing a custom exception, `throw` vs `throws`
- **Java 8+** features — functional interfaces, default methods in interfaces, and Stream API operations like **`map` vs `flatMap`**

### Round 2 — Spring Boot & Hibernate
Shifted to the framework side: **`@Controller` vs `@RestController`**, **CORS** and why it matters in API design, and **`@PathVariable` vs `@RequestParam`**. On the Hibernate side — **ORM** concepts, **eager vs lazy** fetching, and **`get()` vs `load()`**. It closed with a brief, high-level discussion on **microservices** architecture and a few HR questions at the end.

## Verdict
**Rejected.**

title: Microsoft SDE-2 — interviewed for L61, offered L62
excerpt: Four technical rounds covering DSA, SOLID-driven LLD, AI-service architecture and a hiring manager round.
body:
## Background
I focused a lot on getting in front of the right people — leaning on referrals and reaching out to recruiters directly rather than relying on the standard application route.

## Online assessment
Two DSA-heavy problems, one a fairly involved **3D dynamic programming** question.

## Round-by-round
*(Four technical rounds in total.)*

### Round 1 — DSA
Linked lists, priority queues and graphs. The bar wasn't just a working answer — optimal time and space complexity was expected for each problem.

### Round 2 — Low-level design
How well I understood **SOLID** principles and could apply the right design patterns in a real scenario.

### Round 3 — High-level design
Architecture-level thinking: scalability, system optimisation, and specifically how those principles apply when designing AI-driven services.

### Round 4 — Hiring manager
A deeper look at the technical choices I'd made through my career, plus behavioural questions on cultural fit.

## Verdict
**Selected.** I interviewed for an **L61** position but was offered **L62** based on performance across the rounds.

title: Amazon SDE-1 from a Tier-3 college — applying broadly paid off
excerpt: Applied to several SDE-1 openings rather than one. A four-section OA, then three rounds heavy on Leadership Principles.
body:
## Background
I'm from a Tier-3 college, so to maximise my chances I applied to several different SDE-1 openings through Amazon's careers portal rather than pinning everything on one application.

## Online assessment
Four sections: DSA, a work-style assessment (responding to sample workplace emails), a behavioural section, and Leadership Principles questions. The non-DSA sections were where a lot of technically strong candidates seemed to stumble.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1
Conducted by two SDEs together: two DSA problems — one **binary search**, one combining **DP and graphs** — plus behavioural and Leadership Principles questions. I made a conscious effort to stay calm where I got stuck rather than letting it derail the round.

### Round 2
With an SDE-2, starting with a deep dive into past work and projects. Then a hard DSA problem followed by a medium **topological sort** question, with Leadership Principles throughout.

### Round 3
With a senior lead, almost entirely behavioural and Leadership Principles. The technical portion can apparently be skipped at this stage if earlier rounds went well, which seemed to be the case.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Zomato Android Developer — LinkedIn outreach to offer
excerpt: Core Android concepts, then a deeper technical round on DI and KMM, and a cultural-fit conversation about startup environments.
body:
## Background
I relied mostly on **LinkedIn** during my job search — finding relevant postings and sending personalised connection requests to people already working there, which turned out to be a solid way to increase my chances of a referral. I'm a 2025 graduate.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1
About an hour on core Android development concepts — **Activity** and **Fragment** lifecycles, **ViewModels** and **Flows** — plus a few scenario-based questions to see how I'd apply them in practice.

### Round 2
With an engineering manager, and much deeper technically: **Singleton** design patterns, **Dependency Injection**, **Kotlin Multiplatform Mobile (KMM)**, and a detailed discussion of specific projects on my resume.

### Round 3
More conversational — cultural fit, and how genuinely interested I was in working in a startup-like environment.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Amazon SDE off-campus — LRU cache, trees and an SDM round
excerpt: A multi-part OA including a debugging exercise, then two DSA rounds and a behavioural round with an SDM. Offer in 5–6 days.
body:
## Online assessment
Several distinct parts: three coding problems (two medium, one hard) across **dynamic programming**, strings and graphs; a work-style section with situational logic and data-interpretation questions; a debugging exercise working through logs to find the underlying issue; and a slider-based psychometric behavioural section.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA
An **LRU cache** design problem (medium) plus a **binary search** question.

### Round 2 — DSA
A step up: a hard binary tree problem paired with a **graph BFS** question, with time and space complexity expected for both.

### Round 3 — Behavioural (with an SDM)
Entirely focused on the **Leadership Principles**. I'd prepared seven or eight personal stories covering challenges, handling feedback and taking ownership — having them ready made a real difference.

## Verdict
Offer within 5–6 days of the final round. **Selected.**

title: Microsoft SDE-1 on-campus (IIT Roorkee) — resume depth and in-place constraints
excerpt: Two rounds, each opening with a detailed resume deep dive, then medium-level string and array problems with in-place constraints.
body:
## Round 1

### Introduction & resume deep dive
A standard self-introduction covering background and college, then 15–20 minutes on my resume and projects. The interviewer wanted specifics — the tech stack, how each project worked end to end, and what value it delivered. I made sure I could speak to every detail listed, since nothing was off-limits.

### DSA question
A medium-level **string manipulation** problem. I first proposed a solution using a separate string to build the result; the interviewer then added a constraint — solve it **in place**, without extra memory. Once the logic was down they pushed on edge cases: extra spaces at the beginning, at the end and between words. I had to adjust my logic for each.

## Round 2

### Introduction & resume
Another introduction, then a deeper look at my resume — this time weighted toward internship experience and technical projects.

### Core fundamentals
Brief coverage of OOP and DBMS, though the bulk stayed on DSA. On OOP the questions stayed close to encapsulation, polymorphism and virtual classes.

### DSA question 1 — Array manipulation
A medium **array rearrangement** problem: move specific elements to one end while keeping the relative order of the rest. I used an in-place read-and-write pointer strategy and walked through both brute force and the optimised version with complexities.

### DSA question 2 — Tree / graph
A medium tree/graph problem centred on counting a specific type of node.

## Verdict
**Selected.**

title: Accenture — 90 MCQs, a communication check, and a 5-minute interview
excerpt: Three stages that moved faster than expected: an aptitude-plus-coding OA, a spoken communication round, and an interview that lasted barely five minutes.
body:
## Background
Three stages overall, and honestly the whole thing moved faster than I expected once I got into it.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Online assessment
**90 MCQs** covering basic computer knowledge and general problem-solving — nothing too specialised, more a test of overall aptitude. Then two **coding questions**, which I could solve in whichever language I was most comfortable with.

### 2. Communication round
Different from a typical technical assessment. It tested spoken communication through reading passages aloud, listening-and-repeating tasks, and a short **storytelling exercise** based on a topic shown on screen. Less an "interview" than a structured communication check.

### 3. Interview round
Surprisingly brief — just **4–5 minutes**. My background, the project I was most proud of, and since it was relevant to my profile, a few **machine learning** concepts. The interviewer also asked about previous job offers I'd had, which I answered honestly.

## Verdict
**Selected** — the letter of intent arrived within 10 days, with a one-week window to accept.

title: Amazon SDE-1 FTC — cleared the OA, fell short on DP
excerpt: A contract-based SDE-1 role. Cleared a HackerRank OA, then two coding questions on interview day.
body:
## Background
This started with a recruiter call I missed; they followed up by email about a contract-based SDE-1 role. Since it was structured differently from a standard full-time offer, I got clarity on the contract terms up front before moving forward.

## Online assessment
On HackerRank: a fairly basic **dynamic programming** question plus an algorithmic problem combining **binary search** and tree concepts. I cleared this stage.

## Interview day
About two weeks to prepare, then two coding questions.

### Question 1 — Binary search
Manageable on the surface, but the test cases in the round were slightly different from what I expected, which threw me off and made it trickier than it first looked.

### Question 2 — Dynamic programming (medium)
The harder of the two. Looking back I hadn't put in enough targeted practice in this area, and it showed.

## Verdict
**Not selected.**

title: Capgemini on-campus — communication test, tech assessment, and a 20-minute interview
excerpt: An on-campus drive with more layers than expected: a communication assessment, a mixed technical test, and a short video interview on fundamentals. 7.5 LPA role.
body:
## How I applied
Through an **on-campus drive**. The process had more layers to it than I expected going in.

## Round-by-round

### 1. Communication assessment (online)
Not the usual grammar-and-vocabulary test — the format felt genuinely different from anything I'd prepared for elsewhere, so I had to adjust on the spot.

### 2. Technical assessment
A decent spread: **pseudocode**-based questions, core CS fundamentals, and a couple of coding problems mixed in. Nothing wildly difficult, but enough to make sure you weren't coasting on aptitude alone.

### 3. Video interview (15–20 min)
Opened with a self-introduction and drifted naturally into my project work. I spoke about being an evaluator at a **Smart India Hackathon**, which the interviewer was genuinely interested in — it gave the round an easy flow rather than a rapid-fire Q&A.

The technical questions stayed grounded, nothing requiring deep specialisation:
- **Call by reference** in C++
- What **DML** means (DBMS)
- Two **SQL** queries — pattern matching, and counting records in a table
- The classic **Stack vs Queue** comparison
- **APIs** at a conceptual level
- **Encapsulation** from OOP

## Takeaway
For a 7.5 LPA role it stayed surprisingly approachable throughout — nothing designed to trip me up, more a check on whether my fundamentals were solid.

## Verdict
**Selected** — confirmation came about 10 days later.

title: Microsoft SDE-2 via LinkedIn referral — offer one day after the final round
excerpt: Graph-based OA, then trees and DP, an unexpected DSA round in place of LLD, and a notification-service design.
body:
## Background
I applied to Microsoft through a **LinkedIn referral**, with 3.5 years of experience (previously at JP Morgan).

## Online assessment
On HackerRank: two problems centred on **graphs**, medium-to-hard.

## Round-by-round

### Round 1 — DSA
About an hour on **tree** and **dynamic programming** problems — both common themes in Microsoft's process.

### Round 2 — DSA (originally slated as LLD)
I'd prepared for low-level design, but the interviewer pivoted to two more DSA problems: one on **linked lists**, one math-based. Also close to an hour.

### Round 3 — High-level design
Design a **notification service** from the ground up: functional requirements, non-functional requirements and back-of-the-envelope capacity calculations.

A consistent thread across all three rounds: interviewers kept circling back to my previous project work — every round involved a deep dive into what I'd actually built and owned.

## Verdict
An offer one day after the final round. **Selected.**
